title: Boldness and the Childlike State
english: Through the vote and judgment of providence, some things are made manifest and others are not. The [fate] of John became manifest after his death, but of others before death, such as Susanna and Joseph. Even if vengeance occurs here or not, no one seeks whether it is thus or not here; for the judgments of God happen this way; for 'his judgments are unsearchable' (Ps 18:25). Guard my soul and rescue me; let me not be put to shame, for I have hoped in you (Ps 94:19). If you guard my soul without harm or injury, I know that I shall be rescued; for indeed I am rescued from the evildoers or I receive a crown because of having been afflicted. The guileless and the upright clung to me, because I endured you, Lord. Not only did I profit myself by enduring, endurance which brings salvation—for 'the one who endures will be saved unto the end' (Jas 1:12)—but I profited many because I endured you, and I had many friends. But he speaks of the guileless here as those being crushed by malice, not the well-behaved. Thus the upright were joined with them. According to the reception of malice they are guileless, but according to the taking up of virtue they are upright. For example, one who turns away from evil so as to no longer practice it has become guileless. And since after the turning away from evil he receives the doing of good, the one who turns away from evil becomes upright. It is therefore possible to call the same people guileless and upright according to one thought and another. And it is also possible thus: those who are guileless according to practice being outside of malice, while the upright are those who think the things of piety.

Redeem, O God, Israel from all his afflictions. Since He Himself has attained the petition concerning Himself, He wills also for Israel—for every discerning one and possessing mind—to have the same salvation, to become outside of the afflictions through God having redeemed. It is not out of place, then, to take these things also concerning the man of the Lord. Beginning from where we began the psalm, if we have spoken, it is because the things said concerning the man according to the Savior are common to all the righteous, only His being His own in the theological [sense]. Judge me, Lord, for I have walked in my guilelessness. The voice is very bold toward God. But he has boldness toward God, whose heart does not condemn, as the great disciple and evangelist John writes in the epistle: 'if... (1 Jn 3:20)'.

"Our heart does not condemn us; we have boldness toward God." Thus the whole psalm is sent up from much boldness. He speaks of some things as if already accomplished, and of others as present and active, and some things signify a prayer of the speaker; for he says: "Judge me, Lord, for I have walked in iniquity" (Ps 51:3). He did not say "I shall walk," but "I have walked." And here "iniquity" means guilelessness. He who has turned according to the instruction of Jesus and has become as children, he has become in guilelessness, and such a person is perfect in mind, but a child in wickedness, as the apostle writes: "Be perfect in mind, and a child in wickedness" (1 Cor 14:20).

He who is a child in wickedness does not ignore it—for how could he be a child in it if he ignored it?—but he does not act upon it. This is indeed what he says: "In my iniquity I have walked." Thus, here it is different. In both cases the guileful means what was previously said, "turned according to the children." Therefore, he who has turned according to the teaching of Jesus and has become as children does not lack sense. He does not mean the foolishness of infants, but the immobility toward evils. It was said, therefore, that a child sleeping with a woman does not accept her desire. So when someone, having become perfect, has such a state of being without desire for debauchery, he is a child in guilelessness and has become as children having turned. For observe that these children, according to their age, are not such as to be foolish or easy-going. But the perfect one has become such that it is a matter of choice to be thus a child and thus without guile. Regarding infants, this does not appear; it is not a matter of choice, but of an age that does not permit having a perfect intellect.

The "I have walked" here does not speak of an interruption or a stopping, but that I began this way from a long time ago, or I began this way from the womb; for he says: "Upon you I have been leaned from the womb, from my mother's womb you are my covering" (Ps 71:6). And the saints, concerning whom it is said: "Whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son" (Rom 8:29), belong to this boldness. And hoping in God, I shall not be weak. He no longer says "having hoped," as with "I have walked." But the hope toward God makes one strong and very capable. Since, therefore, I hope in you, "I am not weak." Concerning this...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Sacrifice of the Soul and the Meaning of Kidneys and Heart
english: Weakness is often produced by the divine disciplines. 'He brought them'—he says—'them'—evidently the Hebrews—'in gold and silver, and there was no weakness in their tribes.' For when God leads anyone in gold, that is to say, in a pure mind, and in silver—a tested word—there is no weakness. Those led thus do not suffer weakness, but are strong 'in the one strengthening' them. And as the apostle says, 'I can do all things' (Phil 4:13), he who is able to do all things does not suffer weakness; so also each of the wise men who is strong does not suffer weakness. For how could he who says to God in Psalm 92, 'I will love you, O Lord, my strength' (Ps 92:10), suffer weakness? He who hopes in wealth will surely suffer weakness.

And even if the name of weakness signifies sickness—for it does mean—this is what it says: hoping in the Lord, I shall not be sick according to the soul, I am always being healthy; for 'the one keeping the commandment, this one is healthy.' This is not spoken concerning physical health; for many keeping a commandment suffer sickness, and many transgressing commandments are healthy. 2 Test me, O Lord, and try me (Ps 26:2). Behold the boldness; 'refine my kidneys' and see if there is injustice in me. No one is called to examine such hidden things, knowing the marrow, unless he has much boldness. Therefore, some people, because of the excess of the boldness of the one speaking boldly, take the psalm for the man of the Savior. And it has been said to us already many times, that the achievements of the Savior touch the man and all perfect men. 'Test me, O Lord, and try me.' Bring me into the contest. Just as a capable athlete might say to the contest-setter: 'Test me and try me, if I am such a man as I promise.'

To test God in this way means that he is worthy to happen to receive testing from Him. 'But just as we have been tested by God to be believed in the gospel,' 'we were pleased to share with you not only the gospel, but also our own souls' (1 Thess 2:8). Someone shares his own soul with someone when he prepares him according to the quality he possesses. Not only, he says, do we have the readiness to share the gospel with you, but also our own souls. If anyone becomes an imitator of the apostle and has all his disposition and practice, he trans[fers]...

The soul of the apostle is received. This can be grasped easily: for 'we are ready even to risk our lives' because 'he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for one another'. If we, when placing our lives for those we love, were placing some intellectual or allegorical soul, it would be different; but we do this by imitating Jesus, who truly laid down a human and not an allegorical soul.

“Purify my kidneys and my heart. For your mercy is before my eyes, and I have rejoiced in your truth” (Psalm 51:10-14). Behold that through all things he trusts in his own purity. Since these things seem to be beyond human power, he immediately says: “for your mercy is before me” (Psalm 51:14). I know that even if I propose good things, even if I hasten to run after them, if you do not show mercy, I will not be perfected. Therefore, “I have rejoiced in your truth” (Psalm 51:14). One need not be self-deprecating here when the subject is truth. I recall someone saying: if you are asked, “Are you a virgin?”, say: “Because of God, I have been a virgin until now, and I wish to remain a virgin until now through faith, and entirely.” He who rejoices in the truth of God has the mercy of God before his eyes. Having the one who cooperates and perfects before his eyes, he will speak boldly toward those who have already been made upright by him. Therefore I say: “Purify my kidneys and my heart, for your mercy is before my eyes” (Psalm 51:10-14).

The kidneys and the heart are joined together in many places in Scripture: “God tests hearts and kidneys” (Psalm 7:11). “And even until night my kidneys instructed me” (Psalm 16:7). And just as when we hear 'heart', it does not mean the part of the body, but rather the one who has it sees God; again: “Hear me, you who have lost your heart”, no one loses this bodily part in such a way—if not, if God casts out a stony heart and places a fleshy one in its stead, we understand the intellect. Along with this heart, the so-called kidneys are not parts of the body. It is said that the seminal women are first composed there, and from there they easily pass into the sexual organs. Therefore, the kidneys are procreative and ministers of seed.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: True Will and the Seat of Folly
english: Therefore there are also wombs, according to that which the soul or the mind brings forth; those he calls kidneys along with the named heart. 'You are near,' he says, 'to their mouth, but far from their kidneys' (Psalm 51:4). From these kidneys you are far, O God, not from the physical parts. Therefore I have directed my kidneys and my heart, test me (Psalm 51:6). I do not have seeds capable of bearing offspring, such as to become exalted children, destructive children, like those Judas had; for it is said: 'Let them be brought to destruction. Let there be no redeemer for him' (1 Samuel 2:9), nor a helper to his children, not concerning physical children. Perhaps we do not even know if he had children. He calls all the traitors of the truth his children. Just as Paul brings forth through the gospel, he brought forth through the betrayal of those from whom he came in order to hand over Jesus: 'What do you want me to give you, and I will hand him over to you?' (Matthew 26:25). Through this eagerness, he became the father of all the traitors of the truth. 'And I rejoiced in your truth' (Psalm 96:11). The one rejoicing in the truth of God is not ashamed of his words; for Jesus said: 'Whoever is ashamed of me and my words' (Mark 8:38). But if he himself is ashamed of the one being ashamed, the one speaking boldly and remaining in the truth and preferring it above all, he himself is a weakling; let him remain in him.

4 I did not sit with a seat of futility and with law-breakers, I will by no means enter. The evil and the good are not co-existing. The one having the good cannot partake of evil. The one having been set upon evil, insofar as he is evil, is unfit for virtue. And since abstaining from evil—when one, having a nature toward them, abstains from them by choice—the children do not have intemperance, but I do not say they abstain from intemperance. The soulless and the irrational do not have impiety; and I do not say they abstain from impiety; for abstaining is a volitional movement. In the first psalm, therefore, he blesses the man who is perfect according to the inner man: 'Blessed is the man who walked not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of scoffers' (Psalm 1:1). The sophist and deceiver can say that neither the child, nor the irrational, nor the soulless 'walked in the counsel of the ungodly and in...'

"He does not stand in the way of sinners, nor does he sit in the seat of mockers" (Ps 1:1). Denying the perfect man such things, he says: how can one abstain from these by having "his own will in the law of the Lord" (Ps 119:2)? For it is not possible for everyone to have "his own will in the law of the Lord." For those who think they do not sin by returning to the law only because they fear punishment, do not have "their own will in the law of the Lord." If indeed someone were to persuade them that there is no punishment, they would do everything that is forbidden. But he who has "his own will in the law of the Lord," even if a thousand trials and many punishments were hanging over him, does not depart from the will of the law. Such were the Maccabees, such were the witnesses of the truth among us.

Just as he does not previously say that the perfect man abstains from evils by having his own will in the law of the Lord, and having said the appropriate good things here, he then says what is forbidden and says: because I walked in integrity (Ps 26:4) and hoped in you, not having my mercy weak before your eyes, since I am such a person, "I did not sit with a seat of futility" (Ps 26:5). He did not distinguish the futility of the seat by anything other than being in such a life; for life is divided among men, not a place. Diligence divides the serious man from the base men, and knowledge separates the one who has it from the ignorant. So also here, the one who walked in integrity and having hope in God, and because of this being strong and not weak, "did not sit with a seat of futility" (Ps 26:5).

And here one might say: "the child and the irrational and the soulless did not sit with a seat of futility." But they did not sit with a seat of futility because of not being by nature, but because of walking in integrity and hoping in God. "And after those who transgress, I shall by no means enter" (Ps 26:6). I never consented with those who consult in vain and sit in council to do such things, nor did I enter after transgressors. I did not only not sit, but I did not even enter; for after the entrance, the sitting is that which is in the council. Jeremiah also was attaining to this choice and virtue, saying: "I did not sit with those playing, but I was reverent from the face [of God]" (Ps 26:6-7).
